         New Delhi, November 3
     In a significant development, Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In), the Centre’s nodal agency for responding to cybersecurity incidents, has secured access to Anthropic’s advanced artificial intelligence model Claude Mythos to conduct experiments on identifying and potentially exploiting software vulnerabilities, government sources said on Tuesday.
The move comes in the wake of incidents last month in which autonomous AI agents gained unauthorised access to systems belonging to Indian enterprises.
CERT-In is examining the model’s ability not only to detect security vulnerabilities but also to potentially exploit them in controlled environments, allowing the agency to assess the risks posed by increasingly capable AI systems and strengthen India’s cyber defences.
“When you look at what we are doing in cyber security, we have not been able to have access to Mythos. Now CERT-In has just got the access...but we don’t want to send out everything on the cloud and send it all over the place, we better do it in a closed door environment and we are doing it, and we are finding the efficiencies improving. Originally, we were doing it about 60 per cent of what when Mythos came in, but we are closer to about 80-85 per cent now. It is detecting issues, we are able to patch, and we are able to go forward,” a senior government official said.
The access is particularly significant given the cybersecurity concerns raised last month when autonomous AI agents, deployed by AI companies for research and evaluation exercises, accessed live systems of Indian organisations without authorisation.
The official said several organisations, particularly small and medium enterprises, could have suffered serious breaches had CERT-In not intervened to alert them to the vulnerabilities and issue advisories.
“Both in the case of Anthropic and in the case of OpenAI, they themselves found out much later that this thing (model) has escaped, then they started notifying entities across the world as to where they are. The minute it came to India, both of them realised that they all have to tell us —CERT-In — before the entities. So, they told us and simultaneously, but number of months had passed,” the official said.
The incidents have also reinforced the need for companies to strengthen their internal cybersecurity systems and regularly audit their digital infrastructure, the official said.
“When we issued the detailed cybersecurity audit guidelines a year and a half ago, a lot of people came back to us and said this is such a long thing and why are you doing this, but now in the hindsight, I think that was relevant...number of things have been caught through that process,” the official added.

indian-startups-1a7382a05b.headline: Razorpay receives SEBI approval for IPO
indian-startups-1a7382a05b.fulltext:
Fintech unicorn Razorpay has received approval from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) for its initial public offering (IPO), according to sources familiar with the development.
The Bengaluru-based company had confidentially filed its draft red herring prospectus (DRHP) with SEBI in June 2026.
According to an Economic Times report, Razorpay is targeting to raise Rs 5,500-6,500 crore through its IPO at an expected valuation of $5 billion (Rs 49,000-50,000 crore).
As per sources, the company expected to file its final IPO papers before March 2027.
Media reports indicate that Razorpay has roped in Axis Capital, Kotak Mahindra Capital, JP Morgan and Citi as bankers for its proposed IPO.
Razorpay was last valued at $7.5 billion in 2021, when it raised $375 million during the peak of the funding cycle. Since then, the company has undertaken several strategic initiatives ahead of its public market debut.
In April 2025, Razorpay converted into a public limited company as part of its IPO preparations. Later that year, it completed its reverse flip to India, a process that involved shifting its domicile from the US to India. The company paid around $150 million in taxes related to the transition.
Founded in 2014 by Harshil Mathur and Shashank Kumar, Razorpay provides payment gateway services to businesses. Over the years, it has expanded into business banking, lending and payment solutions for merchants.
Most recently, Razorpay received the final Payment Service Provider (PSP) licence from the International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) to operate in GIFT City, Gujarat. The licence will allow the fintech company to offer payment services to businesses operating in the International Financial Services Centre.
Entrackr has reached out to Razorpay for comments. The story will be updated once the company responds.

Fal, a San Francisco-based startup that hosts and runs AI video, image, and audio models, has raised $1.3 billion in its latest funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from Nvidia, Sound Ventures, and T. Rowe Price. The deal values Fal at $16 billion, double its $8 billion valuation in April, Bloomberg reported.
The startup announced its Series E and F rounds at the same time, noting that a combined $1.65 billion was raised across both. (Sequoia led the earlier round.)
The latest round (Series F) comes amid soaring demand for inference services, the process of running an AI model that’s already been trained to generate outputs, particularly from customers relying on open source models. global-economics-5fde059d3d.headline: Apple warns of ‘unprecedented’ rise in memory chip prices
global-economics-5fde059d3d.fulltext:
Apple has warned of an “unprecedented” rise in memory chip prices, as it battles with datacentres to lay its hands on supplies.
The iPhone maker’s shares fell in after-hours trading after it told investors that the higher prices will eat into its profit margins.
“What we’re seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented,” John Ternus, Apple’s new chief executive, told a conference call on Monday, predicting that memory costs in the fourth quarter of this year would be even higher than in the previous three months.
The tech industry has been gripped by “RAMageddon” for months, as demand for memory chips from AI datacentres has surged, driving up prices.
Ternus said Apple’s decision to raise iPad and MacBook prices in June, followed by iPhone prices in September, had “provided some offset” for the company.
Ben Barringer, the head of technology research at Quilter Cheviot, said Apple’s results were “OK, if on the disappointing side”.
“Revenues were up 12%, driven primarily by iPhone sales and strong sales of Mac Mini, which users can use to apply agentic AI. China growth was robust which is pleasing to see, while iPad and wearables disappointed with services growing but lower than the group average at 10%,” he added.
“There appears to be a lot of interest in the iPhone Duo, but it is early days yet with the product not yet on full release, but it is hoped that can help drive the next leg of Apple’s product innovation.”
Apple’s shares were down 2.75% in after-hours trading on Wall Street.
Apple posted stronger-than-expected revenue in the fiscal third quarter, giving Ternus an upbeat start to his tenure, which began in September. The solid results bucked a downward trend for tech companies this quarter, as companies including Alphabet, Amazon and Intel had disappointing quarterly results.
Jacob Bourne, an Emarketer analyst, said record iPhone revenue and strong growth in China demonstrated the resilience of Apple’s business.
Apple earned $30.71bn (£22.89bn), or $2.10 a share, in the July-September period, up 12% from $27.47bn, or $1.85 a share, in the equivalent period a year earlier. Apple said its earnings included five cents a share from tariff refunds.
Revenue rose 12% to $114.5bn from $102.5bn.
Analysts, on average, were expecting earnings of $1.99 a share on revenue of $113.4bn, according to a poll by FactSet.
While its rivals are facing investor uncertainty over huge investments in artificial intelligence, Bourne said Apple’s “tepid approach” to AI infrastructure spending had helped preserve its cashflow – while partnerships with companies such as Alphabet could help the iPhone maker strengthen its AI capabilities without taking on the same financial risks as its peers.

indian-startups-84b9e7e991.headline: ideaForge takes flight as Q2 FY27 revenue jumps 124% to Rs 91 Cr
indian-startups-84b9e7e991.fulltext:
ideaForge achieved a Q2 FY27 financial turnaround with Rs 91.3 crore revenue and Rs 23.2 crore EBITDA, while advancing combat UAVs and securing Rs 151 crore RDI funding for heavy-lift logistics.
Strong execution and technology innovation helped drive a sharp financial turnaround for Indian drone maker ideaForge in the second quarter FY27.
“Building on the steady start of the year in Q1 FY27, Q2 FY27 saw continued progress in order book execution, new product development, and preparations to capitalise on upcoming procurement opportunities,” said Ankit Mehta, Co-founder and Chief Executive Officer of ideaForge Technology.
In Q2 FY27, revenue from operations reached Rs 91.3 crore, up 124% year-on-year (YoY) from Q2 FY26. For the half-year period H1 FY27, operating revenue surged 199% YoY to a record Rs 159.9 crore from Rs 53.5 crore in H1 FY26, driven by delivering over 50% of the opening order book.
Revenue streams were led by the defence vertical, which generated Rs 65.7 crore or 72% of Q2 FY27 operating revenue. The civil and enterprise segment contributed Rs 25.6 crore or 28% in Q2 FY27, driven by mapping projects, crowd safety monitoring, and Drone-as-a-Service software subscriptions, which offer cloud-based drone operations.
The company returned to profitability, reporting a profit after tax (PAT) of Rs 6.5 crore in Q2 FY27, with a net margin of 7.1%. This compares with a loss of Rs 19.6 crore and a negative margin of 48.1% in Q2 FY26.
EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation) stood at Rs 23.2 crore, with a margin of 25.4%, compared with a loss of Rs 8 crore and a negative margin of 19.6% in the year-ago quarter.
Q2 FY27 total expenses rose 41.8% YoY to Rs 90.1 crore. The largest cost centre in Q2 FY27 was material costs at Rs 48.1 crore, representing 53.4% of total expenses, followed by employee benefit expenses of Rs 16.6 crore (18.4%), other expenses of Rs 16.0 crore (17.8%), depreciation and amortisation of Rs 14.7 crore (16.3%), and finance costs of Rs 1.0 crore (1.1%).
“We have maintained our execution momentum despite persistent global supply chain constraints and a few delays in customer approvals for deliveries. While these challenges remain significant, we continue to closely monitor developments and take measures to minimise their impact on our operations and deliveries,” Mehta commented.
The firm secured Rs 151 crore in research debt funding from the Technology Development Board to develop YETI, a middle-mile logistics drone carrying 200 kg payloads over 200 km.
It completed field testing for the ZOLT hybrid tactical drone, offering 100 km range and 6 hours endurance with electronic warfare resilience to withstand signal jamming during intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance missions.
However, hurdles remain with global supply bottlenecks, customer delivery acceptance sign-off delays, and a shrinking order book that stood at Rs 202.2 crore by Q2 FY27 end, down from Rs 350.8 crore in Q3 FY26 as execution outpaced new contract awards.
High working capital intensity also persists, with inventory at Rs 155 crore and trade receivables at Rs 161.1 crore. Nevertheless, an estimated Rs 20,000 crore Fast Track Procurement pipeline offers strong medium-term visibility.

Trump axes US$3.8b annual military aid for Israel: ‘they no longer need it’
US President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that Washington was ending a 10-year security aid deal with Israel that allowed US$3.8 billion in annual aid to its ally until 2028.
Trump said Israel was “fine” with him ending the aid, which began in 2019 and was signed under his predecessor, Barack Obama, three years earlier.
“We’ll help Israel if they need it,” he added in an interview on US current affairs show Fox and Friends, saying that he had agreed with Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to cut the aid.
“Israel’s our No 1; we give them more than anybody else, and they no longer need it … If they did need it, I would say keep it going,” Trump added.
Under the deal, Israel receives funding for the purchase of around US$3.8 billion of weapons a year.
Since its founding in 1948, Israel has received more than US$300 billion, adjusted for inflation, in US economic and military aid, according to figures from the Council on Foreign Relations, far more than any other country has received since 1946.
The Israeli prime minister has previously said he wanted to end Israel’s reliance on US support.
In June, Netanyahu called for his country to increase its military autonomy and reduce its reliance on Washington. In January he told The Economist that he hoped to do so within a decade, while in May he told US broadcaster CBS that he wanted support to reach “zero”.
Netanyahu said in an interview with an Israeli television channel in October: “If you think we’re going to continue receiving what I secured twice, and that’s tens of billions of dollars in American aid for the defence budget, prepare yourselves and get used to the fact that it won’t happen because America has changed.”
On Tuesday, Trump cited attacks by leftist Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for the US Senate in Tuesday’s midterm elections after harnessing popular discontent and anti-Israel sentiment, as part of the reasoning behind the decision.
“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like an El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” he said on Fox, referring to Israel and the aid.
US public support for Israel has fallen since the Gaza war began in 2023, particularly among Democrats.
A June Quinnipiac University poll ‌found 48 per cent of voters and 66 per cent of Democrats believe the US is too supportive of Israel, up from 16 per cent and 20 per cent, respectively, ⁠when the question was first ⁠asked in 2017.
Some members of Trump’s Make America Great Again movement have ⁠also become increasingly critical of Israel, accusing it of having misled Trump – who campaigned in 2024 on a promise to avoid foreign military interventions – into believing Iran could easily be defeated in a war.
Congress passed a law in 2020 authorising the funding for Israel, but ‌the Senate and House of Representatives ‌must still pass appropriations bills every year to distribute and release the funds.

RAJEWADI, India – Indian farmer Amarsingh Gushinge wants to sow wheat and chickpeas in coming weeks to capitalize on attractive prices, but dwindling water supplies after below-average monsoon rains are preventing him from planting either crop.
Like Gushinge, millions of farmers, especially in southern and western India, are facing water shortages as they prepare to plant winter crops.
“There’s not enough moisture in the soil to sow the next crop, and no money left to do so either,” said Gushinge, 78, in the village of Rajewadi, about 400 kilometers east of Mumbai. The Jalna district around his village has received about 48% less rain than average this year, the local weather office has said.

IEA: India Can Help Diversify Global Solar PV Supply Chains
India’s growing solar PV module capacity could strengthen India’s export prospects, despite upstream manufacturing gaps, says IEA in a new report 
Key Takeaways
- India could account for half of global module manufacturing capacity outside China by 2030, according to a new IEA report
- The country could have around 135 GW of surplus module manufacturing capacity available for exports by 2030, but China will continue to dominate
- Battery storage pipeline continues to expand, but financing, technology access, and project execution remain key challenges
India’s expanding solar PV manufacturing industry could play a growing role in diversifying global supply chains, as the country strengthens its position as a major manufacturing hub, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).
In its India Renewable Energy Market Report 2026, the IEA identifies India as the world’s second-largest manufacturer of solar PV modules after China, with annual module manufacturing capacity reaching around 225 GW in September 2026, up from around 22 GW in 2022. It expects the country to maintain this position through 2030 as manufacturing capacity continues to expand, reaching around 250 GW by the end of this decade.
The report notes that India’s growing clean energy manufacturing base is helping diversify international supply chains. This comes as global solar manufacturing remains concentrated in China, particularly in upstream segments of the PV value chain.
The IEA credits India’s industrial policies, including the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) scheme and domestic sourcing requirements, with helping mobilize investment in solar PV manufacturing. New policy measures are also targeting strategic upstream segments, where global dependence on imports from China exceeds 95%, the IEA said.
The report focuses on India’s growing importance in the global renewable energy markets, which reduces its reliance on imported fuels. According to the report’s estimates, India’s coal imports in 2025 would have been around 110 million tons higher without the solar PV, wind, and bioenergy capacity added since 2010. Import dependence for electricity generation would also have exceeded 30%, approximately twice the actual level.
By 2030, the country is forecast to reach around 530 GW of renewable power capacity, with solar PV accounting for more than 80% of new additions. This also opens up new opportunities in the manufacturing space.
The IEA estimates that the country accounted for 40% of global solar module manufacturing capacity outside China and 20% of non-China cell manufacturing capacity in 2025. By 2030, these shares are expected to increase to around 50% and 30%, respectively.
The country’s installed solar PV capacity is likely to exceed 450 GW DC/350 GW AC. Analysts project that by 2030, India could have about 135 GW of surplus solar module manufacturing capacity available for export, making it the world’s second-largest potential exporter after China.
This expansion could create opportunities to serve markets seeking alternatives to Chinese solar PV products, particularly as the European Union and other regions pursue supply chain diversification policies.
China will nevertheless continue to dominate the market with almost 600 GW of spare capacity by the IEA’s estimates. Indian manufacturers will face intense competition in international markets as the report estimates about 780 GW of global module manufacturing capacity will be available for export, against an estimated global import demand of around 130 GW to 160 GW.
Globally, solar PV manufacturing capacity across the supply chain exceeded 1,200 GW in 2025, compared with approximately 630 GW DC of annual installations. China accounted for around 75% of global module manufacturing capacity, 90% of cell capacity, and 95% of wafer and polysilicon capacity.
The IEA expects intense competition in international markets to continue, with Chinese manufacturers retaining a cost advantage. Access to export markets will increasingly depend on cost competitiveness, trade policies, local-content requirements, and supply chain security regulations.
Even as China accounts for the lion’s share of global solar PV manufacturing at lower costs, the IEA estimates India’s integrated solar PV manufacturing costs to reach around $0.15/W, supported by lower labor and energy costs and economies of scale. This would be approximately 10% higher than production costs in China but lower than those in the EU and US without subsidies. However, costs remain around 70% above current global spot market prices, posing a challenge for Indian manufacturers amid global oversupply and intense price competition.
However, the IEA cautions that India’s manufacturing expansion has not been uniform across the PV value chain. While module production capacity has increased rapidly, upstream manufacturing remains underdeveloped.
India’s solar cell imports reached around $2.5 billion in 2025, with approximately 70% sourced from China. Wafer manufacturing was also in its early stages, with the country commissioning its first facility, with around 2 GW of annual capacity, in 2025. India had no operational polysilicon production facility as of 2025.
The IEA expects India’s cell manufacturing capacity to exceed 60 GW by 2030, while wafer capacity could reach around 50 GW based on announced projects. Polysilicon production could also develop sufficiently to support approximately 20 GW of integrated module production annually by the end of the decade.
It identifies technology access, financing requirements, process know-how, scale-up risks and competition from lower-cost imports as challenges to expanding upstream manufacturing. India also remains dependent on imported manufacturing equipment, process technologies and technical expertise, particularly from China.
The IEA also highlights the growing importance of battery energy storage systems (BESS) in supporting India’s renewable energy expansion. As solar and wind capacity increases, storage will be increasingly important for managing variable generation, improving grid flexibility and ensuring a reliable electricity supply.
Battery energy storage deployment in the country is also expected to accelerate, especially during the second half of this decade. According to the IEA, at the beginning of 2026, India’s installed utility-scale battery storage capacity stood at just 350 MW, of which 280 MW was commissioned in 2025.
In 2026, more than 1 GW of additional capacity is expected to come online, with annual installations projected to reach 6 GW to 8 GW by 2030 in line with the growing share of renewable energy. India’s National Electricity Plan sees battery storage capacity rising to nearly 9 GW by 2026-27, and almost 50 GW by 2031-32.
By January 2026, India’s battery storage project pipeline reached around 111 GWh, equivalent to approximately 35 GW of capacity. However, converting announced and tendered projects into operational capacity remains a challenge, the analysts caution, citing financing, grid connectivity, equipment procurement, and project execution as key bottlenecks.
“Improved auction and contract design, accelerated permitting and faster grid connection are critical to converting India’s battery storage pipeline into operating capacity,” recommend the analysts.
The complete IEA report is available on its website for free download.

Huawei tells customers to find their own AI chip memory, effectively outsourcing procurement to the black market
Key Points
- Facing U.S. sanctions and supply shortages, Huawei is directing customers to procure memory for its new AI chips independently on the black market.
- Smugglers dodge U.S. rules by pairing HBM with low-end processors and routing them into China through Hong Kong.
- The shortage has driven black market prices for HBM units to around $4,000, while South Korea reports record levels of illegal chip exports.
Huawei can't get enough memory for its AI chips, pushing customers onto the black market. A sophisticated smuggling network has sprung up to fill the gap, exploiting a loophole in U.S. export rules.
Huawei is telling some customers to source the memory for its AI chips themselves, effectively pushing buyers onto the black market, The Information reports. The company plans to launch the Ascend 960DT early next year, which it says will double the performance of its current chips. But Huawei's Chinese suppliers can't produce enough High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM), and U.S. export rules block direct purchases from Samsung and SK Hynix. Together, those two companies control over 80 percent of the global market.
Smugglers have found a workaround. They bundle HBM with cheap server processors whose performance falls below the export threshold, then ship the packages to China through Hong Kong. Once there, workshops separate the memory chips from the processors. The process is fragile and the error rate is high, but the margins make it worth it.
Smuggled memory prices have surged to $4,000 per unit
Prices for smuggled HBM3E memory have jumped from a few hundred dollars to around $4,000 per unit in just one year, according to a broker in Shenzhen. Each AI chip needs six to eight units, meaning the memory alone can cost up to $32,000.
The black market doesn't run on smuggling alone. Older Nvidia GPUs stripped for parts and excess inventory from chip designers who scrapped projects or cut orders also feed the supply. South Korea's customs authority had uncovered trade violations worth $560 million by May, already surpassing the previous full-year record. A third of that total involved strategic goods like chips exported without proper authorization or with false declarations.

On the evening of Sunday, November 1, 2026, I spotted a white Delhi Police SUV marked “Facial Recognition System” and “South District” parked near the entrance of Nexus Select Citywalk, the mall in South Delhi’s Saket District Centre. I photographed it while walking past it, feeling mildly concerned and definitely uncomfortable.
My lawyer friends, now used to being surveilled everywhere, scoffed at it, as I wondered what it could be doing here, so far from protest sites, which is where they are publicly known to be. Whether any of the cameras on it were turned on or not, or whether it was simply parked there is information I could not confirm. MediaNama could not find any public announcement of a facial recognition vehicle for South District. Moreover, I saw no sign at the spot saying facial recognition was in use. So, this is not based on assumptions, but simply on information available to us publicly. Additionally, I have also written to the Delhi Police with questions about the rest.
We have blurred the face of a person standing in front of the vehicle, because we do not know whether they have any connection to it. Two faces in the background have also been blurred.
DP-DRISTHI: The Shahdara district police launched this vehicle at Gandhi Nagar market in February 2026. It “can scan several faces in a minute and match them with the police database of criminals having previous involvements”, The Tribune reported. “By deploying this mobile unit, the Shahdara District police aim to create a ‘zero-blind-spot’ environment in commercial hubs,” Deputy Commissioner of Police (Shahdara) Prashant Gautam said at the launch.
Ikshana: This was described as a “live CCTV surveillance vehicle” by a senior Delhi Police officer, and was inducted ahead of the G20 Summit in 2023, ThePrint reported. The feeds in Ikshana use facial recognition software, and it was spotted at Jantar Mantar during the protests in July, according to The Tribune.
There seem to be a plan to increase these surveillance vehicles as Delhi Police invited bids worth Rs 15.66 crore for 338 cameras with face recognition across Central and New Delhi districts on July 30, 2026, the Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) reported after reviewing the tender.
This system has only been described by the Delhi Police in context of the Jantar Mantar protests in an affidavit before the Supreme Court in August. It was said that the system flagged 2,873 people with prior records over seven days, and that it did not “automatically capture, create, generate or maintain profiles of every individual present at the protest site”, MediaNama reported. While Delhi Police has not revealed which datasets populate the system, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta told the courts that no actions are taken automatically after a match is made.
There seem to be no specific statutes, or any published standard operating procedures (SOPs) which MediaNama could find that governs police use of facial recognition in Delhi. In the Supreme Court’s 2017 privacy judgment of the K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India case, it was said that there needs to be a law-backed mandate for any state intrusions into privacy, serving legitimate aims while being proportionate. However, the government can exempt state agencies from the provisions of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, but it has not come into force yet entirely.
MediaNama is tracking and researching facial recognition technology being used by law enforcement agencies.
If you have seen a Delhi Police facial recognition vehicle at a mall, market or metro station, or anywhere else outside a protest or official event site, please write to us at anjali@medianama.com. Please include the date, time and place, alongside any photos, as this would help us collate legitimate data.
Delhi Police had not responded at the time of publishing. This post will be updated if it does.

Fourth-quarter revenue will be $17 billion, plus or minus 3%, the chipmaker said in a statement Tuesday. That easily topped the average analyst estimate of $16.3 billion, helping send the shares up about 7% in late trading. 
  November 04, 2026 / 06:34 IST  
Advanced Micro Devices Inc., a key challenger to Nvidia Corp. in artificial intelligence chips, gave a sales forecast that soared past analysts’ projections, a sign of buoyant demand for data center processors.
The outlook provided fresh evidence that AI spending is sustainable, soothing jittery investors. Shares of chipmakers and other tech companies have been battered in recent weeks over concerns about a bubble in the AI infrastructure industry.
“AMD’s earnings are simultaneously a test of its own performance and of the broader AI trade,” Emarketer analyst Jacob Bourne said in a note. The results “will give investors encouragement given the recent tech and semiconductor selloff, as investors increasingly scrutinize AI spending and its returns.”
AMD’s outlook — along with a strong forecast from server maker Super Micro Computer Inc. — helped spark a late-trading rally among AI equipment makers and cloud providers. Shares of companies from CoreWeave Inc. and Nebius Group NV to Dell Technologies Inc. and Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co. all gained.
Under Chief Executive Officer Lisa Su, AMD has become one of the most important suppliers of processors and computers that operate at the heart of AI facilities, underpinning a flood of new services.
Even with recent market turbulence, AMD shares have more than doubled this year. The company’s valuation reached $1 trillion in September, putting it in an elite group.
The data center growth has helped AMD offset a slump in the personal computer market, where rising memory-chip costs have slowed production and depressed user demand. Intel Corp., AMD’s top rival in that field, suffered its worst stock decline in decades after a downbeat earnings report last week.
One possible weak spot for AMD: Its gross margin will narrow to about 55% in the fourth quarter. That measure — the percentage of sales after removing production costs — had been 56% in the previous period.
On a conference call with anlysts, Su said the company has become more optimistic about long-term growth. It expects revenue to increase more than 80% next year, outpacing the 75% expansion seen by Wall Street. Sales from data centers will more than double, accounting for as much as 80% of total revenue.
The company “has strong confidence in our ability to sustain exceptional revenue growth for years to come, with earnings growing even faster,” Su said.
AMD’s third-quarter sales rose 45% to $13.4 billion. Profit climbed to $2.09 a share, minus certain items. Analysts on average had predicted revenue of $13.1 billion and earnings of $1.97 a share.
AMD continues to deliver record results and now boasts sales that are twice as big as they were two years ago. It’s also been outperforming longtime nemesis Intel in the market for central processing units, or CPUs. But the company is still well behind Nvidia in so-called AI accelerators, which are used to train and run artificial intelligence models.
Sales at AMD’s data center business nearly doubled to $8.5 billion. Analysts had predicted a total of $8.2 billion. PC and gaming-related sales shrank 8% to $3.7 billion.
Like other makers of components for PCs, AMD is suffering from a side effect of the data center boom. AI servers require a massive amount of memory. That’s cut into the supply of chips available for laptops and desktop machines — and forced prices up. The total PC market will decline by a double-digit percentage next year, Su said during the conference call.
AMD is debuting new product ranges in both the CPU and accelerator markets. The Santa Clara, California-based company is also taking on Nvidia more directly with its Helios server design.
But Nvidia, the largest chipmaker and world’s most valuable company, hasn’t been standing still. It’s updating its own lineup at a fast pace and branching out into everything from software to networking to complete computers.

deep-tech-01f87ea7de.headline: Is There Room for Small-Scale OSATs in India’s Chip Packaging Boom?
deep-tech-01f87ea7de.fulltext:
Small OSATs in India can start with ₹1.5–₹2 billion (~$15.8–$21 million), consultant Nitin Dodia said. But anchor customers, skilled staff, and qualification determine who survives.
India’s expanding outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) industry is creating opportunities for smaller, specialized packaging facilities alongside large, capital-intensive plants. Sahasra Semiconductors’ operating facility in Bhiwadi, Rajasthan, represents one such entry point, with an investment of more than ₹1.5 billion (~$15.8 million), according to a May 2026 government announcement.
The question is whether smaller facilities can build commercially viable businesses by focusing on mature packaging technologies and specific product segments.
EE Times spoke with Nitin Dodia, semiconductor consultant and founder-director of Smart Fab Systems, who estimated that a facility focused on mature packaging technologies could be established with an investment of ₹1.5 billion (~$15.8 million) to ₹2 billion (~$21 million). He said the amount would depend on the products handled, equipment requirements, and operating expenditure.
Dodia’s estimate applies mainly to mature, non-advanced products with simpler processes. “Simple wire bonding or leadframe-based packaging is less capital-intensive,” he said.
Production volume drives capital expenditure (capex), Dodia said. A company such as Micron processes millions of chips every month and needs equipment built for those volumes. OSATs handling specialized products with mature technologies can start with much lower capex.
Sahasra’s semiconductor packaging facility, set up under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology’s Scheme for Promotion of Manufacturing of Electronic Components and Semiconductors (SPECS), spans 5,295 square meters (57,000 square feet) and has a stated annual packaging capacity of 60 million units. It packages memory chips for microSD cards and flash storage, LED driver ICs, eSIMs, and RFID products. The government described Sahasra as India’s first small and medium enterprise (SME) to begin commercial production of semiconductor chips.
RRP Electronics operates an OSAT facility in Mahape, Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra, serving automotive, industrial, and telecom customers.
The larger OSATs work on a different scale. Tata Electronics’ ₹270 billion (~$3.25 billion) OSAT facility in Assam has an approved capacity of 48 million units a day. CG Power’s ₹76 billion (~$910 million) facility in Sanand, Gujarat, has a planned capacity of 15 million units a day. Kaynes Technology’s ₹33.07 billion (~$395 million) facility, also in Sanand, is designed to handle more than 6.33 million units a day. By comparison, Sahasra’s stated annual capacity of 60 million units translates into an average of about 164,000 units a day.
“The bigger point, however, is that success is not just about money,” Dodia said. “Whether you are setting up a smaller or a larger operation, you need to find an anchor customer.” He also pointed to capacity utilization, experienced personnel, and product qualification as key factors.
Dodia said a new OSAT should secure at least one customer committed to buying its products over three to five years. This matters even more when the initial investment is low.
Companies such as Sahasra and RRP Electronics have an advantage because they entered the market earlier and already have customers buying their products. “That matters more than simply investing the money,” Dodia said. An investor could spend ₹1 billion (~$11 million) to ₹2 billion (~$21 million) on equipment. But if the equipment sits idle because no customers are lined up, the investment will not deliver the expected returns.
Larger players such as CG Semi and Kaynes Semicon follow the same model, with anchor customers and technology partners. Renesas, for example, is both a technology partner and an anchor customer for CG Semi, whose initial production serves Renesas’s packaging requirements. “Without that arrangement, there is little point in proceeding,” Dodia said.
Dodia said a buyer such as Apple or Samsung might have to work with 10 smaller OSATs, each with capacity tied to a ₹1 billion (~$11 million) to ₹2 billion (~$21 million) investment, to meet its requirements. “This creates additional management work for the customer as well,” he said.
Dodia said capacity utilization matters more than initial capex. Equipment is expensive whether a company invests ₹1 billion (~$11 million) or ₹10 billion (~$105.4 million). Idle equipment ties up money, and the company continues to pay interest. “Therefore, what matters most is whether your products and equipment are being utilized to their fullest potential,” he said.
Investors also need patience. Dodia said returns are typically zero in the first year, and investors should not expect returns in the first two or three years.
“In my view, the workforce, particularly experienced personnel, is the most underestimated requirement,” Dodia said.
Suppliers can provide quotes for equipment and material costs, he said, but experienced personnel is scarce worldwide. Indian OSATs compete for talent with the U.S. and other countries expanding chip manufacturing to reduce dependence on external suppliers.
Dodia expects the pool of experienced personnel to run dry. Much manufacturing knowledge is not documented. Two identical tools from the same vendor can behave differently over time as residue builds up in their process chambers. An experienced engineer can read statistical process control (SPC) charts and find the cause. AI cannot help without the data. “Most of the time, the knowledge exists in someone’s head,” Dodia said.
In an earlier interview with EE Times, Wasi Uddin, senior manager of R&D and training at Kaynes Semicon and a former OSAT and ATMP consultant at MeitY, said the “immediate gap is not materials or equipment; it is the expertise required to operate semiconductor-grade manufacturing facilities.” He said most of this expertise comes from the Philippines and Malaysia, or from Indian engineers who worked abroad and returned. Semiconductor manufacturers also have to compete with the IT sector on engineer salaries, he said.
Product qualification is the second hurdle, Dodia said. Qualification cycles often take 12 to 24 months, so a new OSAT cannot supply customers as soon as it installs equipment. A customer may ask for six or 12 consistent batches before it qualifies a supplier. Even then, the OSAT may serve only as a secondary supplier. Material suppliers can spend about 12 months qualifying with an OSAT.
Dodia said smaller OSATs should ideally operate in clusters. Instead, states compete for semiconductor investment, and plants are spreading across the country. India has approved 12 projects under the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM). Dodia said a chemical supplier serving these plants and companies such as RRP Electronics may need warehouses in eight or 10 locations. Some materials, such as leadframes for certain relatively advanced packages, must come from within a few hundred kilometers of the OSAT because transport can affect them.
Tata has one plant in Dholera, Gujarat, and another in Assam, so its suppliers must manage logistics from west to east. Dodia acknowledged that states have reasons to share in the industry. But he said supply chains will take longer to mature. “Something that could have taken three years may now take five years,” he said.
Sanand in Gujarat shows the alternative. Dodia said Gujarat has three OSATs in Sanand and three more in the surrounding areas. One supplier facility nearby can serve three companies.
Uddin said that OSATs can import materials for the first three to five years while local suppliers build up. “Why is there no leadframe supplier till now in India? Because there was no OSAT, there was no market,” he said.
“Micron, CG Semi, and Kaynes formed a consortium and held monthly supplier meetings so suppliers could see their combined demand,” he said.
Commodity packaging puts smaller OSATs in competition with suppliers worldwide, Dodia said. Large OSATs, meanwhile, are directing their growth toward advanced packaging. Amkor’s advanced packaging revenue rose to $5.56 billion in 2025, while its mainstream wirebond business stayed flat at $1.15 billion.
Large OSATs also retire some older package lines. In 2022, ASE’s Chung-Li plant in Taiwan decommissioned its punch quad flat no-lead (QFN) line, forcing NXP to withdraw two parts.
Dodia sees an opportunity for smaller OSATs in these discontinued products. “Many products have such well-established applications that demand continues for 10 to 20 years. Automotive is one example,” he said. NXP has committed to supplying several automotive microcontroller families for more than 15 years, while Rohm Semiconductor specifies supply periods of 10 to 20 years for some products, including automotive MOSFETs.
He cautioned against crowding. If five or 10 smaller OSATs all target automotive, they will compete in the same race. “Ideally, they should coordinate their efforts, with one company targeting one segment and another focusing on a different segment,” he said. Some could pursue advanced packaging if they have the right customers, since startups and R&D teams often want newer technologies.
Uddin said the major OSAT players have already split by segment. Micron packages memory. CG Semi focuses on legacy packages such as QFN and thin shrink small outline packages (TSSOP). Kaynes focuses on power packaging, and Alpha and Omega Semiconductor has booked 28% of its capacity. “It will be a competition, that is for sure, but it will not be a throat-cutting kind of a competition,” he said.
Dodia said some customers pay a premium for dedicated capacity. Defense customers do not want their products exposed elsewhere and may pay more for a dedicated line. R&D teams and startups need small volumes quickly. When a larger manufacturer receives an order worth millions of dollars, a $10,000 order can wait for months. In all of these cases, time may matter more than unit cost.
Dodia said fabless startups are probably the best customers for new Indian OSATs. Serving them needs a flexible model that supports tens of processes, because their volumes are low and their requirements change fast. Integrated device manufacturers (IDMs) and electronics manufacturing services (EMS) companies could also become customers.
Global companies such as Renesas have two reasons to qualify a smaller Indian OSAT, Dodia said. Incentives could help it offer better prices. A dedicated partner also offers planned capacity for three to five years, without competing against the hundreds of customers that ASE or Amkor serve.
Dodia said India needs a tiered ecosystem, with large OSATs handling high volumes and smaller ones serving customers who need faster turnaround, greater security, or specialized services. Some mature markets abroad already follow this approach. If the ecosystem serves only high-volume customers, startups, defense customers, and R&D teams will not get what they need. “We definitely need both types of OSATs,” he said. Older products and mature technologies can meet many Indian requirements.

global-economics-ca2a9069b4.headline: Who is Dan Driscoll? OpenAI hires ex-US Army Secretary and Trump's 'drone guy' to lead national security AI push
global-economics-ca2a9069b4.fulltext:
LivemintPublished3 Nov 2026, 06:28 PM IST
OpenAI has appointed former US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll as its senior counsellor for national security modernisation, as the artificial intelligence company looks to expand the use of advanced AI in defence and cybersecurity.
The company announced the appointment on Monday, creating a new role in which Driscoll will advise OpenAI's leadership and its public- and private-sector partners on deploying AI to strengthen national security and cyber resilience.
According to OpenAI, Driscoll will work with governments, industry, academic institutions and US allies to identify practical applications of AI in national security.
Driscoll will also help the company's teams understand the operational requirements of security institutions worldwide.
The youngest-ever army secretary, 39-year-old Dan Driscoll, was often referred to as President Donald Trump's 'drone guy' for his embrace of emerging battlefield technologies. An Iraq war veteran, tech investor and former adviser to Vice President JD Vance, Driscoll was nominated by Trump in 2024. The president called him “a disruptor and change agent”. Driscoll resigned in September.
Dan Driscoll previously served as the 26th Secretary of the US Army, overseeing the service's operations, modernisation and resources.
His responsibilities extended to nearly one million active-duty, National Guard and Reserve soldiers, along with more than 265,000 civilian employees, OpenAI said.
During his tenure, Driscoll focused on accelerating the adoption of emerging technologies, reforming military procurement processes and modernising the US Army.
He has also served as acting director of the US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), adding to his experience in government and national security institutions.
Driscoll's appointment comes as OpenAI seeks to strengthen its engagement with defence establishments and explore how advanced AI systems can be integrated into national security operations.
In his new role, Driscoll will advise public- and private-sector partners on policy and strategic changes that could accelerate the adoption of AI in national security.
Driscoll said military personnel needed better tools to respond to rapidly evolving national security challenges.
"The people who serve deserve the very best tools we can put in their hands," he said.
He added that AI could help military personnel reduce administrative workloads, process larger volumes of information and ensure that relevant information reaches the right people more quickly.
Driscoll said he was joining OpenAI to help the US and its allies adopt the technology responsibly.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the US had an opportunity to work with other countries to expand the adoption of what he described as "democratic AI" and strengthen American leadership in the field.
Driscoll's appointment also builds on OpenAI's Daybreak programme, an initiative through which the company is working with allies and partners to strengthen cybersecurity and protect essential services.
The programme focuses on helping organisations identify and address software vulnerabilities before malicious actors can exploit them.
This includes efforts to improve cyber resilience among critical infrastructure providers and institutions that could face growing digital threats.
Through the initiative and Driscoll's appointment, OpenAI is looking to deepen its engagement with governments and security institutions while exploring how AI can support national security, cybersecurity and the protection of critical infrastructure.

climate-energy-6d3ac5bf58.fulltext:
State of the climate: 2026 likely to tie with 2024 as the warmest year on record
With three-quarters of the year now past, it is virtually certain that 2026 will be the warmest or second-warmest year on record.
A rapidly strengthening El Niño, alongside human-caused global warming, made this year’s August the warmest on record and September the second-warmest.
El Niño is the warm phase of a recurring climate pattern in the tropical Pacific that releases heat from the ocean into the atmosphere and temporarily boosts global temperatures.
Carbon Brief’s analysis gives 2026 a 67% chance of surpassing 2024 as the warmest year on record across an average of six global temperature datasets.
In January, it is likely the groups that report global surface temperatures will be divided on whether 2026 officially beat 2024’s record.
Currently, the odds for a record year range from as high as 97% in Berkeley Earth’s dataset to less than 20% in European Copernicus/ECMWF’s ERA5 reanalysis product.
With El Niño expected to intensify into the winter, Carbon Brief projects that 2027 will be 1.7C above pre-industrial levels, with a 96% chance that it is the warmest year on record.
In this latest “state of the climate” quarterly update, Carbon Brief finds:
- August 2026 was the warmest August on record in all six major datasets, at around 0.12C above the previous record. September was the second-warmest September, behind 2023.
- January-September was the second-warmest such period on record, at around 1.45C above pre-industrial levels, behind only 2024.
- El Niño broke the daily “Niño3.4” region record in September and has stayed above the previous record every day since. Nearly all forecast model runs have it as the strongest El Niño on record, with a peak of around 4C occurring this winter.
- Around 22% of the world’s surface saw its warmest July-September on record, including much of the tropical Pacific, the western Mediterranean and Iberia. Western Europe had its hottest summer on record and Spain its warmest September, beating the previous record by 0.7C.
- Carbon Brief projects that 2026 will end up around 1.52C above pre-industrial levels, with a 67% chance of beating 2024’s record.
- Whether 2026 is declared the warmest year depends on the dataset; a record is likely in Berkeley Earth and NASA GISTEMP, is too close to call in HadCRUT5, JRA-3Q and NOAA and is unlikely in ERA5.
- Earth’s energy imbalance has more than doubled since the start of the satellite record, from around 0.5 watts per metre squared (W/m2) in the 2000s to around 1.25W/m2 over the past decade.
- The Arctic sea ice minimum was tied for 10th lowest in the satellite record, while Antarctic sea ice saw its third-lowest winter peak.
- This year’s record-setting El Niño will have its largest effect on global temperatures in 2027. Carbon Brief projects 2027 at around 1.7C above pre-industrial levels, with a 96% chance that it will be the warmest year on record.
A record August and the second-warmest year to date
Carbon Brief analyses records from six different groups that report global surface temperatures:
- NASA’s GISTEMP
- NOAAGlobalTemp
- The Met Office Hadley Centre and University of East Anglia’s HadCRUT5
- Berkeley Earth
- Copernicus/ECMWF’s ERA5 reanalysis product
- The Japan Meteorological Agency’s JRA-3Q reanalysis product
There are a number of additional groups that feature in Carbon Brief’s annual “state of the climate” update, but are not included here due to a lack of regular monthly updates.
The first nine months of 2026 were the second warmest on record in all six datasets, behind only 2024.
The figure below shows annual temperatures in each dataset since 1970, along with the 2026 average to date.
The year got off to a comparatively slow start. Each month from January to June ran cooler than the same month in 2024, as the lingering effects of weak La Niña conditions gave way to a developing El Niño.
La Niña and El Nino are the cool and warm phases of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a recurring climate pattern in the tropical Pacific that reshapes weather patterns around the world.
That changed in the third quarter of the year. July 2026 was the second-warmest July in the six-dataset average and a narrow record in the NASA GISTEMP and NOAA datasets. (NOAA’s own assessment described it as tied with July 2024.)
August then set a new record for the month by around 0.12C in the six-dataset average. It was the warmest August on record in every one of the six datasets, by margins ranging from 0.07C (HadCRUT5 and NOAA) to 0.13C (ERA5).
September temperatures stalled a little following the rise in July and August. At around 1.62C, it was the second-warmest September on record in all five datasets to have reported so far, around 0.08C below the record set in September 2023.
The figure below shows each month of 2026 alongside every year since 1940, with 2023, 2024 and 2025 highlighted.
Across the six-dataset average, July-September 2026 was effectively tied with the same period in 2023 as the warmest on record, at around 1.57C. It ranked first in GISTEMP and NOAA (and in HadCRUT5 for July-August), and second in Berkeley Earth, ERA5 and JRA-3Q.
The figure below shows the January-September average for every year since 1850. It shows how temperatures in 2026 to date sit at 1.45C – around 0.06C below 2024.
A record-setting El Niño event
In September, El Niño crossed a milestone. The daily sea surface temperature anomaly in the “Niño3.4” region of the tropical Pacific – the area most widely used to gauge El Niño strength – broke the record, previously set in November 2015, to become the strongest event since the satellite era began in 1981.
This year’s El Niño has remained above that record every day since. September recorded the highest monthly Niño3.4 region temperature anomaly since records began in the mid-1800s.
As of 18 October, the daily value stood at around 3.5C above the 1996-2025 average for the time of year and around 0.4C above the 2015 peak.
The figure below shows how El Nino is projected to keep intensifying until the end of this year.
Carbon Brief examined 656 forecasts from 14 different climate models that were run between late September and mid-October. On average they estimate that this year’s El Niño will peak around 4C in December – more than 1C above the prior record.
(Ten models expect a December peak and four anticipate a November peak.)
Based on an analysis of tree rings and coral sediments, it is possible that this will be the strongest El Niño event in a millennium.
The forecasts have strengthened since Carbon Brief’s July “state of the climate” update, when El Niño was expected to peak around 3.6C.
While human emissions of CO2 and other greenhouse gases are responsible for effectively all of the Earth’s long-term warming, temperatures in any given year are strongly influenced by short-term variations to the Earth’s climate associated with El Niño and La Niña events.
Global temperatures tend to lag the tropical Pacific by around three months, which means an El Niño peaking around the end of 2026 will have its largest effect on global temperatures in 2027.
Record heat across much of the world
In addition to high global average surface temperatures, the past three months have seen records broken across many parts of the planet.
The map below shows July-September 2026 temperatures relative to the 1981-2010 average in the ERA5 reanalysis.
Globally, temperatures were 0.96C above that 30-year period and 1.58C above the ERA5 1850-1900 pre-industrial average.
The El Niño is clearly visible as a band of exceptional warmth stretching across the eastern and central tropical Pacific, with temperatures more than 4C above average off the coast of Ecuador and Peru.
Western Europe and the Mediterranean were also unusually warm, with temperatures around 3C above average over France and the western Mediterranean Sea. North-west Russia, the Canadian Arctic, south-central North America, eastern Africa and parts of west Antarctica were also exceptionally warm.
The most notable part of the planet that was colder than usual was the Weddell Sea sector of Antarctica, which came in at more than 2C below average for the season.
The map below shows how July-September 2026 ranked against every year in the ERA5 record (1940-2026) at each location. Areas in dark red saw their warmest July-September on record; blues show areas among the five coldest.
Around 22% of the world’s surface saw its warmest July-September on record and around half experienced one of its five warmest. By contrast, around 0.5% of the world saw one of its five coldest July-September periods.
Record warmth covered most of the El Niño region (including more than 90% of the Niño3 and Niño3.4 regions) along with sizeable parts of the south Atlantic (39%), the tropical Indian Ocean (34%) and the subtropical North Atlantic (25%, with 85% in its five warmest).
On land, around 85% of France and Iberia saw a record-warm July-September.
In September alone, around 20% of the world’s surface saw its warmest September on record.
Overall, 55 countries set national records for September average temperatures, including Chile, Colombia, Italy, Kenya, Nigeria, the Philippines, Portugal, Spain, the United Arab Emirates, US and Venezuela.
Europe had an exceptional summer, with the western part of the continent experiencing its hottest summer on record.
Copernicus reported that western Europe’s summer averaged 21.7C – 2.5C above the 1991-2020 average – beating the previous record set in 2003. A record 52% of the continent was exposed to “very strong” heat stress by the end of the season.
Europe as a whole had its third-warmest summer, behind 2024 and 2022.
France had its warmest July on record, at 3.8C above the 1991-2020 average. Switzerland had its hottest summer since records began, averaging 17.2C.
The heat persisted into the autumn in south-west Europe. Spain had its warmest September on record, at 3.4C above the 1991-2020 average. This beat the previous record set in 1987 by a remarkable 0.7C.
Rivers across Europe saw their lowest summer flows since the European Flood Awareness System’s records began in 1992. By early September, the area burned across the EU was almost twice the 2006-25 average for the time of year, according to Copernicus, extending what had already been a severe fire season.
Elsewhere, the contiguous US had its hottest summer on record and its warmest September, with around 59% of the country in drought conditions.
India’s monsoon, which tends to weaken during El Niño years, ended with 12.6% less rainfall than normal, the driest in 11 years.
This year’s El Niño event has strongly impacted the hurricane season, suppressing the formation of hurricanes in the Atlantic while contributing to a record-setting number of tropical cyclones in the Pacific.
Good odds of being world’s warmest year
Carbon Brief’s projection for average global temperature for 2026 combines observed temperatures through September with the latest forecasts of the strength of El Niño. It uses a statistical model trained on the historical relationship between year-to-date temperatures, El Niño conditions and annual temperatures.

The best estimate for 2026 is now around 1.52C above pre-industrial levels, with a 90% range of 1.50C to 1.55C. This is slightly higher – but effectively tied with – the prior record of 1.52C set in 2024.

agritech-f21fd9b84e.headline: Global Farm Support Hits Record US$950 Billion; India’s Net Support to Farmers Remains Negative
agritech-f21fd9b84e.fulltext:
Key Details
The OECD’s Agricultural Policy Monitoring and Evaluation 2026 measures both budgetary support and the effects of policies that change domestic farm prices relative to international reference prices. That distinction is central to its India findings.
The Producer Support Estimate combines these price effects with payments to farmers. A negative estimate does not mean each farmer paid a tax or received a lower price for every crop.
Farm Support and Farm Prices Pull in Opposite Directions
India provides substantial support through subsidised fertiliser, electricity and irrigation water, as well as direct payments such as PM-KISAN. Yet the OECD estimates that domestic marketing rules and trade measures depress prices for a number of products relative to international benchmarks. Across 2023–25, those negative price effects exceeded both positive price support for other commodities and budget payments to producers.
This is an aggregate result, not a uniform experience. The report identifies positive support for commodities including wheat, maize and sugar. India’s negative producer-support estimate also became less pronounced in 2025, although the provisional annual figure remained below zero.
Cheaper Food for Consumers Is Part of the Same Picture
Policies that hold down farm prices can benefit food buyers. India’s Targeted Public Distribution System provides additional budget-funded food support. Combining the relevant price effects and subsidies, the OECD estimates positive consumer support averaging 26.5% of consumption expenditure at farm-gate prices in 2023–25. This percentage does not represent food subsidies alone.
The competing effects explain why changing agricultural support is difficult: a measure that improves producer prices may raise costs for consumers, while a measure that contains food prices may reduce returns to some farmers.
Rising Global Spending Has Not Reversed Slower Productivity Growth
Across the countries studied, agricultural support has risen, but nearly half remains in forms the OECD considers potentially highly distorting. Meanwhile, global agricultural total factor productivity growth slowed from 1.8% a year in 1991–2000 to 0.8% in 2014–23. Spending on shared services—including research, innovation and infrastructure—has grown in absolute terms but declined relative to agricultural production.
In India, general-services spending averaged 4.3% of agricultural production value in 2023–25, with about 85% directed to infrastructure, particularly irrigation. The OECD argues for stronger investment in knowledge, market access and resilience alongside more coherent support for farmers.
Policy Relevance
India’s farm policy must serve small producers and food consumers at the same time. The OECD’s estimates show why adding another subsidy cannot be judged in isolation: its benefit to farmers may be offset by price and trade policies affecting the crops they sell. Equally, easing price restrictions without regard to staple-food affordability could shift costs onto households.
The report recommends improving agricultural markets, including e-NAM and state-level marketing reforms, making export rules more predictable, and gradually redirecting some input support towards productivity and sustainable resource use. The pace and design matter: small farmers need workable access to markets, finance and alternatives before existing support is reduced.

india-ff1472f7e9.headline: India may need to spend 3% of GDP on climate adaptation, against 0.5% in rich economies: Report
india-ff1472f7e9.fulltext:
The study examines 20 established adaptation measures addressing heat, drought, flooding and wildfires, including air-conditioning, irrigation, drainage systems and flood defences.
Why does India face a higher adaptation bill?
According to McKinsey, around 60% of India's population already lives in areas experiencing heat stress, yet air-conditioning coverage remains at approximately 10%.
By comparison, only 4% of the US population currently faces heat stress, while air-conditioning coverage exceeds 90%.
This disparity illustrates the scale of India's infrastructure requirements, particularly for affordable cooling, climate-resilient housing and protection for outdoor workers.
Globally, McKinsey estimates that annual spending required to provide developed-economy protection standards could reach $1.2 trillion by 2050 under a 2°C warming scenario.
Heat stress alone could account for approximately $568 billion, making cooling one of the largest adaptation investment categories.
Why is financing a bigger challenge for India?
The report estimates that less than 20% of India's adaptation investment requirements are deployment-ready, compared with more than half in higher-income regions.
Deployment-ready projects are those with sufficiently clear demand and limited financing barriers to proceed without major interventions.
For India, the remaining investment requirements face obstacles including affordability constraints, competing expenditure priorities and difficulties accessing finance.
McKinsey identifies counterparty risk as a major financing barrier across India, Sub-Saharan Africa and Emerging Asia, affecting measures representing roughly 75% of adaptation costs in these regions.
This makes mobilising capital particularly challenging, even when projects deliver substantial economic and social benefits.
Can private investment bridge the gap?
McKinsey estimates that private companies and households could account for approximately 50% of the world's $1.2 trillion annual adaptation requirement.
Governments could account for another 30%, while the remaining 20% could involve either public or private investment.
However, many climate protection projects do not generate predictable revenues, making them difficult to finance commercially.
The report highlights the importance of innovative financing structures, stronger incentives and measures that reduce implementation costs.
What does this mean for India's economy?
Globally, only $190 billion is currently spent annually on the 20 adaptation measures examined, compared with $540 billion needed to address existing climate risks.
McKinsey estimates that adaptation investments generate benefits worth approximately three times their costs through avoided infrastructure damage, productivity losses and adverse health impacts.
For India, the challenge is therefore not simply identifying economically beneficial projects, but making them affordable and financeable.
Expanding access to low-cost cooling, improving urban drainage and strengthening climate-resilient infrastructure could become increasingly important as the country balances fiscal priorities with rising climate risks.

India has concluded eight trade agreements over the past six years and is negotiating more than 10 others, as it seeks to diversify trade and widen market access for domestic exporters. In the current financial year, it has implemented three free trade agreements (FTAs), with Oman, the United Kingdom (UK) and New Zealand. 
 The agreements currently in force cover exports worth $120.9 billion, or 27.4 per cent of India’s total merchandise exports of $441.5 billion in FY26. Once all agreements under negotiation are concluded, the coverage could rise to 74.5 per cent, equivalent to $329 billion in exports.
 The India-European Union (EU) FTA is among the key deals in the pipeline. Its implementation, targeted for early 2027, is expected to expand preferential access for Indian exporters. India and the EU concluded negotiations in January and are aiming to sign the agreement in December. 
 New Delhi is also negotiating a bilateral trade agreement (BTA) with the US, alongside deals with several other partners. The negotiations cover the US, Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Mercosur, Qatar, Bangladesh, Peru, Canada, Chile, Israel and the Maldives, as well as a proposed trade deal with the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), comprising Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Bahrain.
 The expansion would also widen preferential access for imports. Existing FTAs cover 33.1 per cent of India’s imports, a share that could rise to 67 per cent if all ongoing negotiations conclude. Across exports and imports, the share of trade covered by preferential arrangements could increase from 31 per cent currently to 69.7 per cent.

Investing.com -- US officials have delayed approval for American chipmaking equipment that SK Hynix needs to expand production in China, creating obstacles for the South Korean company's plans to build new memory-chip plants in New York, Reuters reported Tuesday citing people familiar with the matter.
The company is seeking US export licenses to equip its Dalian plant and has argued that increased production at that facility would help fund its planned US expansion. The Commerce Department has not yet approved the new licenses, the report said.
SK Hynix's New York-listed shares briefly slipped roughly 1% lower following the report.
SK Hynix's Solidigm unit reportedly plans to invest about $45 billion to build two NAND plants in Marcy, New York. The investment could potentially reach about $100 billion over time. NAND is memory that retains data when power is turned off and is used for storage in data centers.
The negotiations raise questions about how the Trump administration will balance national security measures designed to keep US technology from aiding China's military against efforts to bring foreign investment and chipmaking to the United States.
Executives from Solidigm are said to have met nearly 10 times with Commerce Department officials since late August. The company needs to ramp up production and develop more advanced NAND chipmaking in China to generate revenue for building a US facility and to remain competitive.
In a meeting last week, Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler maintained his position that the US would not allow more American chipmaking tools to upgrade or expand capacity, one source said. The department has not formally denied a license to export American equipment to fill empty clean space in Dalian. The two sides are also negotiating a separate license for 2027 for equipment to maintain the Dalian facility.
In a statement last week, Solidigm said it regularly evaluates strategic alternatives to serve its customers and enhance its competitiveness. The company said it is exploring options for building a NAND memory fab at potential locations around the world, but no decision regarding any specific course of action has been made.

The Naukri JobSpeak Index rose to 2,836 in October from 2,480 a year earlier. “Diwali fell in October last year, and the holiday weeks pulled hiring down, which gives this October’s index a higher jump,” the online recruitment platform owned by Info Edge (India) Ltd said in a news release.

“Some of October’s growth reflects last year’s festive-season base, and we should read it in that light. What’s encouraging is the kind of hiring we’re seeing,” said Info Edge chief executive Hitesh Oberoi. “Manufacturing companies are building capacity, and demand for AI skills remains strong, indicative of the selective, fundamentals-led nature of hiring demand.”
Within the auto sector, hiring for production and manufacturing roles rose 41%, research and development increased 53% and procurement and supply chain grew 50%. Sales and business development roles saw subdued growth at 7%.
“Auto companies are adding people to design, source and build vehicles at a much faster rate than they are adding people to sell them,” Naukri said.
A similar trend was seen in other industries as well. In industrial products/heavy machinery, production hiring grew 40% and quality assurance rose 41%. In the construction/engineering/cement/metals sector, production roles rose 33%, followed by project and programme management (25%) and site engineering (20%).
“The FMCG sector grew a modest 6% overall, yet hiring for its production functions rose 40% and procurement 20%. Sales and business development hiring in FMCG fell 5%,” the report said.

Among metros, Hyderabad led in white-collar hiring at 15%, followed by Pune (14%) and Delhi-NCR (13%). Bengaluru and Mumbai posted 12% growth each, and Chennai 11%. Kolkata was flat.

“We were giving them $4bn … But it gets cut off at the end of the year,” he said.
Trump also indicated that he had decided to end the aid – which he claimed would be replaced by arms sales to Israel instead – because it had become a popular criticism of US foreign policy led by outspoken candidates including the Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.
“Why should we suffer the slings from lunatics like El-Sayed when they don’t need it?” Trump said. “It’s a bad talking point.”
During the interview, Trump claimed that the abrupt ending of aid was proposed by Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. “We give them $4bn of things and money, and they don’t need it,” he said. “And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and we’ve been talking about it for a couple of years because it’s a lot of money.”
Netanyahu had previously suggested tapering off US military aid to Israel over the next decade, but Trump’s announcement on Tuesday would significantly accelerate that timeline.
Israeli officials appeared to be taken by surprise by the announcement, and leading members of the opposition said it showed the damage that Netanyahu had done to the US-Israel relationship. The announcement comes at a crucial moment after Netanyahu’s party lost its majority in the Knesset in last week’s elections and the opposition is trying to cobble together a coalition to replace him.
“The fact that the security establishment, along with Israeli citizens, is learning about a change in the strategic relationship framework through the media highlights just how much Benjamin Netanyahu’s conduct poses a genuine danger,” said Gadi Eisenkot, a centre-right rival to Netanyahu who is seeking to replace him as prime minister. “We can no longer rely on him and must replace him.”
“A responsible prime minister would have fought to increase American aid, not dismantle it,” wrote Yair Golan, the head of the Democrats opposition party. “Netanyahu is deepening the security and economic crisis, putting Israel’s future at risk.”
Israel received most of the approximately $3.8bn in 2025 as foreign military financing grants that allow the country to buy US military hardware including F-35 fighter jets. Another $500m was given for joint missile defence programmes.
Trump’s announcement on Tuesday appeared timed to affect the outcome of the midterm elections, in which US foreign policy and support for Israel have played an unusually important role in key races, including the Michigan senatorial race where El-Sayed is running against Republican Mike Rogers. El-Sayed would become the country’s first Muslim senator if he is elected.
A Quinnipiac University poll released in September showed that 48% of Americans believed that the US was too supportive of Israel, and other recent polls have shown a historic shift away from US support for Israel and Netanyahu’s government.
Anger over the humanitarian crisis in Gaza has helped usher in a wave of progressive Democratic candidates including El-Sayed, and Trump’s vice-president, JD Vance, has openly accused Israel of trying to sabotage US negotiations with Iran. In a June interview with the New York Times, Vance said of Israel’s foreign policy: “You can’t just kill your way out of solving every single national security problem that you have.”
During his Fox News interview, Trump spoke warmly about Netanyahu and also boasted about his own popularity in Israel. “If people ever got tired of me in the US, I’ll move to Israel and become prime minister,” he said.

India
Weak monsoon, El Niño threaten prolonged food inflation in India  
Inadequate soil moisture is making it difficult for farmers in southern and western India to prepare for winter crops, while rising feed, transport and energy costs are adding to food prices. 
Hyderabad: India is staring at a prolonged period of food inflation as inadequate monsoon rainfall, declining water availability and the threat of El Niño raise concerns over agricultural output. Farmers, especially in the southern and western parts of the country, are facing difficulties preparing for the winter cropping season because of insufficient moisture in the soil.
The impact is already being felt across food markets, with prices of essential commodities such as sugar, pulses, wheat, rice, onions, milk and poultry products witnessing an increase. India Ratings and Research estimates that food inflation could touch around 10% in the October-December quarter.
The rising cost of animal feed, transportation, packaging and energy is further adding to the price burden on protein-rich food products, including chicken, milk and eggs. In the poultry sector, corn and soybean together account for nearly 60-70% of production costs, putting additional pressure on producers.
Chicken prices could see another increase from January as production expenses climb and supplies become tighter. Economists have cautioned that a prolonged rise in protein prices could hit low-income households particularly hard, potentially compelling families to cut down on nutritious food consumption.
The pressure on food prices is also being compounded by restricted sugar production, elevated international commodity prices, a depreciating rupee and higher freight charges.
While India has surplus stocks of rice and wheat, the availability of preferred varieties of these grains remains constrained in certain regions. Economists have warned that sustained food inflation could affect household spending and add to the pressure on the Reserve Bank of India to increase interest rates.
The direction of food prices in the coming months will largely depend on winter crop output and weather conditions.
